analysis.one_liner: Requires gas station pumps to adjust fuel volume for temperature so drivers get a full gallon's worth of energy.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee assignment: with no cosponsors and no action after its referral, it died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Gasoline expands when it is hot, so a 'gallon' pumped on a warm day contains less energy than a gallon at the standard 60-degree reference temperature. The bill would require new and eventually all fuel pumps at retail stations to automatically correct measured volume to that 60-degree standard, with annual inspections, $5,000 fines for noncompliant pumps, and small federal grants of up to $1,000 per pump to help independent station owners pay for the equipment. Small rural stations dispensing under 360,000 gallons a year would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists, especially in warm-weather states, who today can pay for a full gallon but receive less energy in it; the bill makes the measured volume match the standard so what is dispensed matches what is paid for.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers buying gasoline at retail pumps

how_it_helps.text: Requires all new and, within five years of final regulations, all existing fuel dispensers at retail stations to automatically compensate for fuel temperature, so the volume sold equals the volume the fuel would occupy at 60 degrees Fahrenheit.

Requires state inspectors to check pumps annually and report noncompliance to the FTC, with $5,000 fines per noncompliant dispenser and an additional $5,000 if a follow-up inspection finds the pump still out of compliance.

Creates a trust fund from fines and Treasury transfers that funds grants of up to $1,000 per dispenser (capped at $10,000 per recipient) to station owners with five or fewer locations, to offset equipment installation costs, and reimburses states for inspection costs.
Exempts small-volume rural stations that dispense fewer than 360,000 gallons per year from the retrofit requirement, sparing the smallest operations.

analysis.who_pays: Retail fuel station owners, who must buy and install temperature compensation equipment (partly offset by federal grants for small operators), and fuel wholesalers or refiners, whose product can no longer be sold with uncompensated hot-fuel shrinkage; costs may be partly passed to consumers at the pump.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas station owners and fuel suppliers

drawbacks.text: The equipment is not free: station owners must pay for retrofitting pumps, and the bill caps grants at $1,000 per dispenser and only for owners of five or fewer stations, so chains and mid-size operators bear the full cost and may pass it on through higher pump prices.

The per-customer benefit is small. Temperature-related 'shrinkage' is a modest percentage of fuel volume and varies by climate and season, so for many drivers the correction would change pump readings only slightly, and the bill allows states to adopt equivalent or stricter standards, creating a patchwork of measurement rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real measurement inequity — drivers effectively pay the same for less energy when fuel is warm — and it softens the burden on small station owners with grants and a rural exemption. But the per-driver benefit is modest and would show up mostly in warm states, while the equipment mandate's costs fall on station owners immediately. It is a defensible consumer-fairness fix rather than a major cost-of-living measure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator McCaskill introduced the FAIR Fuel Act on July 21, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was ever taken on the bill, and it drew zero cosponsors.
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, without the Senate Commerce Committee reporting the bill or the Senate voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Station owners and fuel suppliers who benefit from uncompensated hot-fuel sales are better off because the bill never advanced; drivers gained nothing and lost nothing, since the current measuring rules stayed in place.

for.name: Sen. Claire McCaskill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Jay Rockefeller (D-WV)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup and never reported the bill, leaving it without a path to a Senate vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so its support was a single Democrat with no visible opposition bloc in the record.

industries.note: Station owners must buy and install temperature-compensating pumps and face $5,000 fines per noncompliant dispenser, but owners of five or fewer stations get federal grants up to $1,000 per pump, and small rural stations are exempt. Drivers are their customers, so a fairer pump also protects them from accusations of short-selling fuel.

Without temperature compensation, warm fuel dispensed at retail contains less energy per gallon, so the seller effectively delivers less product for the same price; a mandated 60-degree standard eliminates that quiet gain and shifts more real energy content to the customer.
A federal mandate for automatic temperature compensation on every new and eventually every existing pump would create a large guaranteed market for manufacturers of that equipment.
